## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.102230.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.102230.3.sa2)

The data is largely electrophysiological recordings coupled with behavioral measurements (technically impressive) and some gain-of-function experiments in freely walking flies. Loss-of-function was tested but has minimal effect, which is not surprising in a system with partially redundant control mechanisms. The data is also consistent with/complementary to subsequent manuscripts (Yang 2023, Feng 2024, and Ros 2024) showing additional descending neurons with contributions to steering in walking and flying.

The experiments are well executed, the results interesting, and the description clear. Some hypotheses based on connectome anatomy are tested: the insights on the pre-synaptic side - how sensory and central complex heading circuits converge onto these DNs is stronger than the suggestions about biomechanical mechanisms for how turning happens on the motor side.

Of particular interest is the idea that different sensory cues can converge on a common motor program. The turn-toward or turn-away mechanism is initiated by valence rather than whether the stimulus was odor or temperature or memory of heading. The idea that animals chose a direction based on external sensory information and then maintain that direction as a heading through a more internal, goal-based memory mechanism, is interesting but it is hard to separate conclusively.

The "see-saw", where left-right symmetry is broken to allow a turn, presumably by excitation on one side and inhibition of the other leg motor modules, is interesting but not well explained here. How hyperpolarization affects motor outputs is not clear.

The statement near Figure 5B that "DNa02 activity was higher on the side ipsilateral to the attractive stimulus, but contralateral to the aversive stimulus" is really important - and only possible to see because of the dual recordings.

Comments on revisions:

I am happy that the revised manuscript addresses all reviewers' concerns.

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.102230.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.102230.3.sa3)

Summary:

Rayshubskiy et al. performed whole-cell recordings from descending neurons (DNs) of fruit-flies to characterize their role in steering. Two DNs implicated in "walking control" and "steering control" by previous studies (Namiki et al., 2018, Cande et al., 2018, Chen et al., 2018) were chosen by the authors for further characterization. In-vivo whole-cell recordings from DNa01 and DNa02 showed that their activity predicts spontaneous ipsilateral turning events. The recordings also showed that while DNa02 predicts transient turns DNa01 predicts slow sustained turns. However, optogenetic activation or inactivation showed relatively subtle phenotypes for both neurons (consistent with data in other recent preprints, Yang et al 2023 and Feng et al 2024). The authors also further characterized DNa02 with respect to its inputs and show functional connection with olfactory and thermosensory inputs as well as with the head-direction system. DNa01 is not characterized to this extent.

Strengths:

(1). In-vivo recordings and especially dual recordings are extremely challenging in Drosophila and provide a much higher resolution DN characterization than other recent studies which have relied on behavior or calcium imaging. Especially impressive are the simultaneous recordings from bilateral DNs (Fig. 3). These bilateral recordings show clearly that DNa02 cells not only fire more during ipsilateral turning events but that they get inhibited during contralateral turns. In-line with this observation, the difference between left and right DNa02 neuronal activity is a much better predictor of turning events compared to individual DNa02 activity.

(2). Another technical feat in this work is driving local excitation in the head-direction neuronal ensemble (PEN-1 neurons), while simultaneously imaging its activity and performing whole-cell recordings from DNa02 (Fig. 4). This impressive approach provided a way to causally relate changes in the head-direction system to DNa02 activity. Indeed, DNa02 activity could predict the rate at which an artificially triggered bump in the PEN-1 ring-attractor returns to its previous stable point.

(3). The authors also support the above observations with connectomics analysis and provide circuit motifs that can explain how head direction system (as well as external olfactory/thermal stimuli) communicated with DNa02. All these results unequivocally put DNa02 as an essential DN in steering control, both during exploratory navigation as well as stimulus directed turns.

Weaknesses:

While this study makes a compelling case for the importance of DNa02 in steering control, the role of DNa01 on the other hand seems unclear based on physiology, optogenetics perturbations as well as connectome analysis. DNa01 still remains a bit mysterious regarding both its role in controlling steering maneuvers as well as what in behavioral context it would be relevant.

results.result: DNa01 and DNa02 project to all three leg neuromeres in the ventral nerve cord, forming selective connections onto leg-control networks. DNa02 makes more direct synaptic connections onto motor neurons compared to DNa01, and very few postsynaptic cells are shared between the two DN types.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C6, and C7 are well-supported by citations to published connectome studies (Braun et al., 2024; Cheong et al., 2023) and are illustrated in Figures 1A-C. The anatomical and connectome data provide strong evidence for the distinct projection patterns and synaptic targets of these two descending neuron types.

results.result: Both DNa01 and DNa02 are depolarized before ipsilateral steering and hyperpolarized when the fly stops moving. DNa02 exhibits more transient fluctuations and its spike rate fluctuations typically precede those of DNa01.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1D and E. The temporal dynamics and correlation patterns between the two neuron types are clearly demonstrated in the data, establishing their distinct but coordinated roles in steering control.

results.result: DNa01 and DNa02 firing rate increases predict large changes in rotational and sideways velocity but not forward velocity. DNa02 operates with higher gain than DNa01, with larger and biphasic steering filters compared to DNa01's monophasic filters, suggesting DNa02 produces more transient steering changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C19 are supported by linear filter analysis shown in Figures 2A-E. The computational analysis of neural-behavioral relationships is methodologically sound, with appropriate normalization and statistical validation. The biphasic vs. monophasic filter distinction (C16-C18) is clearly demonstrated and correctly interpreted in terms of signal processing principles.

results.result: DNa02 fires more transiently than DNa01 and is recruited earlier. Even after normalizing for firing rate dynamics, the behavioral impulse response is more transient for DNa02, making it associated with more transient steering events compared to DNa01.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 synthesize findings from Figures 1D-E and 2A-B. The temporal precedence and transient nature of DNa02 activity are well-documented in the data. The normalization approach strengthens the conclusion that the transient behavioral responses are not solely due to transient neural firing patterns.

results.result: Rotational velocity is a steeper function of DNa02 activity compared to DNa01 activity, supporting a higher-gain relationship between DNa02 activity and steering.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by data in Figures 2F-H. The gain analysis is consistent with earlier filter analysis results and provides converging evidence for functional specialization. However, the analysis would benefit from quantitative slope comparisons with statistical tests.

results.result: Rotational velocity is linearly related to the right-left difference in DNa02 firing rates across the entire dynamic range, consistent during both forward and backward walking. Similar results were obtained for DNa01. Bilateral DNa02 predictions accurately predict turns in both directions, and the neural networks presynaptic to these DNs are organized to recruit both ipsilateral excitation and contralateral inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C34 are supported by dual recording experiments shown in Figures 3A-E and supplementary figures. The linear relationship is well-characterized with n=4 flies. The inference about ipsilateral excitation and contralateral inhibition (C33-C34) is reasonable given the bilateral recording data, though C34 is forward-looking to connectome analysis presented later.

results.result: Head direction neurons (EPG neurons) can influence steering via central complex neurons. The central complex contains no DNs but has strong anatomical pathways to DNa02, motivating the hypothesis that DNa02 participates in steering toward internal goals.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 are supported by multiple citations establishing the role of EPG neurons and central complex in steering (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Giraldo et al., 2018; Green et al., 2019; and others). The anatomical connectivity to DNa02 is documented in cited studies (Hulse et al., 2021; Mussells Pires et al., 2024; Rayshubskiy et al., 2020; Westeinde et al., 2024). The hypothesis (C38) is a reasonable inference from this prior work.

results.result: PEN1 neurons relay angular velocity information to EPG neurons, and micro-stimulating them causes the head direction system to register a fictive turn. The EPG bump represents working memory of heading direction and jumps to a new location upon PEN1 stimulation, with bump jumps rarely occurring in genetic controls lacking the Gal4 transgene.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 describe established knowledge about the head direction system (C39-C42) supported by citations (Green et al., 2017, 2019; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Turner-Evans et al., 2017) and experimental validation (C43-C44) shown in Figure 4B. The negative control (C44) is essential and properly executed.

results.result: Following EPG bump jumps, flies execute compensatory behavioral turns that return the bump to its initial location in 40% of trials. The turn direction is appropriate to return the bump via the shortest path (clockwise jumps → rightward turns, counter-clockwise jumps → leftward turns), indicating the mechanism is sensitive to error direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 are supported by experimental data in Figures 4C-D and are consistent with prior work (Green et al., 2019). The directional specificity of compensatory turns is well-documented. The 40% success rate (C46) indicates variable but consistent behavior. The inference about error direction sensitivity (C50) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: DNa02 fires bursts just before compensatory behavioral turns that return the EPG bump to its initial location. The sequence is: bump jump → increased DNa02 firing on the appropriate side → steering maneuver → bump return. DNa02 predicts trial-to-trial variability in turn magnitude and is recruited specifically on the side predicting turn direction, not bilaterally.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C57 are supported by data in Figures 4E-H. The temporal sequence and side-specificity of DNa02 activation are clearly demonstrated. The predictive power for trial-to-trial variability (C53) strengthens the causal interpretation. The negative control trials (C54-C55) and the inference about specificity (C56-C57) are well-supported.

results.result: DNa02 activity predicts the magnitude and direction of steering maneuvers guided by the head direction system, arguing that pathways from the head direction system to DNa02 are functionally strong and recruited at appropriate times to mediate steering commands from the central complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 synthesize findings from the head direction experiments. The functional strength of the pathway (C59-C60) is a reasonable inference from the predictive power and timing of DNa02 activation, though direct causal manipulation of this specific pathway would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Lateralized fictive odor stimuli produce steering toward the stimulated antenna and asymmetric DNa02 responses with higher firing rates ipsilaterally. Stimuli often produce contralateral hyperpolarization, suggesting ipsilateral excitation is accompanied by contralateral inhibition. Genetic controls lacking the LexA transgene show no response.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The behavioral and neural responses are consistent with prior work (Borst and Heisenberg, 1982; Gaudry et al., 2013). The negative control (C65) is essential. The inference about contralateral inhibition (C64) is reasonable but would benefit from more direct evidence.

results.result: Fictive heat stimuli drive behavioral turning away from the stimulus and produce DNa02 responses with higher firing rates contralateral to the stimulus. DNa02 activity is higher ipsilateral to attractive stimuli but contralateral to aversive stimuli, encoding the laterality of the stimulus-evoked action rather than the stimulus itself.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by data in Figure 5B. The contrast between attractive and aversive stimulus responses (C68) is particularly important for establishing that DNa02 encodes action direction rather than stimulus location (C69). This is a key functional insight well-supported by the data.

results.result: DNa02 is activated ~150ms before stimulus-evoked turns and predicts trial-to-trial variability in turn magnitude, suggesting it participates in reorienting the body in response to lateralized stimuli. Similar results were obtained for DNa01.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by data in Figures 5C-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The temporal precedence (C70) and predictive power (C71) support a causal role. The similarity between DNa01 and DNa02 responses (C73) suggests coordinated function, consistent with earlier findings.

results.result: DNa02 hyperpolarizes when the fly stops walking but continues responding to lateralized odors during immobility with similar stimulus-evoked firing rate changes as during walking, suggesting DNa02 contains information about latent steering drives even in quiescent behavioral states.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by data in Figures 6A-D. The persistence of sensory responses during immobility (C75-C76) is well-documented. The interpretation as latent steering drives (C77) is a reasonable inference, though the authors acknowledge alternative explanations (small undetected postural changes).

results.result: DNa02 integrates multiple types of steering signals: internal goal-directed signals from the central complex, stimulus-directed signals from olfactory and thermosensory systems, and locomotor state signals that depolarize the cell during walking.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 synthesize findings from multiple experiments (Figures 4-6). Each type of input is well-documented experimentally. This integration is a key finding establishing DNa02 as a convergence point for diverse steering control signals.

results.result: The inputs to DNa02 are largely non-overlapping with those of DNa01, consistent with DNa02 being recruited before DNa01 with more transient activity. Both DNs receive substantial input from central brain intrinsic neurons, but only DNa02 receives direct input from PFL3 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by connectome analysis shown in Figure 7A-B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The non-overlapping inputs (C82) explain the functional differences observed in earlier experiments. The selective PFL3 input to DNa02 (C85) is consistent with its role in head-direction-guided steering.

results.result: PFL3 cells compare head direction with internal goal signals and produce directional steering commands when there is a mismatch. PFL3 neurons are the likely origin of turning signals in DNa02 during chemogenetic injection of error signals into the head direction system.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by multiple citations (Dan et al., 2024; Goulard et al., 2021; Hulse et al., 2021; and others). The inference that PFL3 is the origin of turning signals (C88) is reasonable given the direct connectivity and the experimental results in Figure 4, though it remains an inference.

results.result: PFL3 neurons send strong indirect projections to DNa02 via DNa03 and LAL010 (ipsilateral excitation) and via inhibitory interneurons (contralateral inhibition). This architecture suggests a 'see-saw' model of steering where excitation of one DN is accompanied by inhibition of the contralateral DN, consistent with observed responses to lateralized stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 are supported by connectome analysis in Figure 7C-D. The see-saw model (C95) is a well-supported inference from the connectivity pattern and is consistent with experimental observations (C96). The amplification via indirect connections (C91) and contralateral suppression (C93) are reasonable functional predictions from the anatomy.

results.result: Some indirect connections onto DNa02 are bilaterally symmetric. DNa03 and LAL010 receive strong bilaterally symmetric projections from PFL2, which is recruited when the fly is oriented away from its internal goal and increases steering gain without specifying turn direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are supported by connectome analysis in Figure 7E and citation to Westeinde et al., 2024. The bilateral symmetry (C97-C98) contrasts with the asymmetric PFL3 connections, suggesting different functional roles. The PFL2 function (C99-C100) is from cited work.

results.result: Multiple pathways connect olfactory and thermosensory peripheral cells to DNa02, with the shortest involving mushroom body output neuron MBON32. MBON32 projections are organized for see-saw steering and could drive turning toward appetitive stimuli as well as away from aversive stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 are supported by connectome analysis in Figure 7F-H and citation to Li et al., 2020. The see-saw organization (C103) is consistent with the PFL3 pattern. The bidirectional function (C104) is an inference from connectivity that is elaborated in subsequent claims.

results.result: Two parallel pathways connect antennal lobe projection neurons to MBON32: a plastic excitatory pathway (via Kenyon Cells) and a fixed inhibitory pathway. Depression of KC→MBON32 synapses by aversive stimuli (via dopamine neuron PPL103) could unmask inhibition, allowing appetitive stimuli to excite MBON32 (driving ipsiversive turning) while aversive stimuli inhibit MBON32 (driving contraversive turning).
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are based on established knowledge of mushroom body circuitry (C105) and cited work on synaptic plasticity (C107: Cohn et al., 2015; Hige et al., 2015; Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Li et al., 2020; Perisse et al., 2016). The functional predictions (C108-C109) are reasonable inferences from this circuitry and are consistent with the behavioral observations in Figure 5.

results.result: DNa02 receives abundant visual input from multiple sources: visual projection neurons from the optic lobe, projection neurons in the anterior optic tubercle downstream from LC10 cells (small object motion detectors), and via MBON32 which receives multimodal sensory input.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 are supported by connectome analysis shown in Figure 7A and F, with citations to Li et al., 2020 (C111) and work on LC10 cells (C113: Hindmarsh Sten et al., 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2018; Schretter et al., 2025). The multimodal convergence onto DNa02 is well-documented.

results.result: DNa02 is a site of integration for many steering control pathways arranged for see-saw steering control. Many pathways involve parallel excitation and inhibition, which could specify steering direction based on E/I balance. When one pathway is plastic, changes in E/I balance could convert memory recall into bidirectional behavioral readout.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 synthesize connectome findings and are well-supported by Figures 7C-F. The E/I balance mechanism (C117) is a reasonable inference. However, C118 is more speculative, proposing a general principle for memory-guided behavior that extends beyond the direct evidence, though it is consistent with the MBON32 circuitry described.

results.result: Unilateral optogenetic activation of DNa02 evoked a small but statistically significant steering bias in the ipsilateral direction, as determined by comparison with a bootstrap simulation using bilateral expression controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by data in Figures 8B-C. The statistical approach using bootstrap simulation with bilateral controls is appropriate and rigorous. The effect size is small but significant, consistent with DNa02 being one of multiple steering DNs.

results.result: Bilateral inhibition of DNa01 significantly reduced sideways speed, but surprisingly, rotational speed was unchanged when either DNa01 or DNa02 neurons were inhibited.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C122 are supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments in Figure 8E. The lack of effect on rotational speed (C122) is surprising given the strong correlations observed in earlier experiments, but this is acknowledged and explained by the authors in terms of compensatory mechanisms and multiple steering DNs.

results.result: Body rotation can be achieved via many different leg maneuvers. Inhibiting DNa01 produced a significant defect in inner-back-leg stance prolongation (pivoting), with a similar trend for DNa02. This defect appears to be compensated by other mechanisms to achieve normal rotational movement in freely moving flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 are supported by leg kinematics analysis in Figures 8F-G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1, with C123 supported by citations (DeAngelis et al., 2019; Katsov et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2024). The compensatory mechanism inference (C127) is reasonable given the unchanged rotational speed despite specific leg maneuver defects. The analysis is methodologically sound with appropriate statistical corrections.

results.result: Bilateral inhibition of either DNa01 or DNa02 altered leg movement rhythm (increased step length, decreased step frequency) regardless of walking direction. Inhibiting DNa01 also decreased forward velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 are supported by data in Figure 8H. The effects on step parameters are consistent across both DN types, suggesting shared functions. The forward velocity effect for DNa01 (C130) is interesting given the weak correlation with forward velocity during normal locomotion.

results.result: Both DNs can lengthen the stance phase of the ipsilateral back leg and/or decrease step length in ipsilateral legs, either of which would promote ipsiversive turning.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 are inferences from the optogenetic inhibition results. While the stance prolongation effect (C131) has direct support from Figure 8G, the step length effect (C132) is more speculative. The authors appropriately express caution about these interpretations, noting the effects are weak and off-target expression is possible.

results.result: DNa01 and DNa02 are both recruited during turning but receive largely non-overlapping inputs and have non-overlapping outputs, representing parallel and independent pathways. DNa02 predicts large, rapid, transient steering events while DNa01 predicts smaller, slower events. DNa02 is recruited earlier with more transient firing. These results argue for specialized roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C140 synthesize major findings from electrophysiology (Figures 1-2) and connectome analysis (Figure 7). The functional specialization is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches. This is a central conclusion of the paper.

results.result: Both DNs can lengthen ipsilateral back leg stance phase and/or decrease ipsilateral leg step length, promoting ipsiversive turning. DNa02 receives stronger and more direct input from some steering circuits in the brain compared to DNa01.
results.evaluation: Claim C141 synthesizes optogenetic findings (Figures 8G-H) with appropriate caution. Claim C142 is supported by connectome analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1. Together these help explain why DNa02 predicts larger steering events.

results.result: Subsequent studies (Yang et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2024; Braun et al., 2024) confirmed that unilateral DNa02 excitation produces ipsilateral body rotation, bilateral DNa02 ablation reduces corrective turning velocity in head direction tasks, and bilateral activation of DNa02 or DNa01 can drive turning in either direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 cite subsequent work that confirms and extends the current study's findings. These provide independent validation of key results. The citations are appropriate and strengthen confidence in the main findings.

results.result: Yang et al., 2023 found that perturbing DNa02 mainly affected ipsilateral leg movements, while DNa02 activity during voluntary turns correlated with both ipsi- and contralateral legs with opposite changes. The brain connectome analyses in this study explain this effect through the see-saw arrangement of inputs producing concurrent excitation of one copy and inhibition of the other.
results.evaluation: Claim C146 cites Yang et al., 2023. Claim C147 is a reasonable inference connecting the cited work with the connectome analysis in Figure 7. This demonstrates how the anatomical findings explain functional observations from other studies.

results.result: Yang et al., 2023 found unilateral DNa02 inhibition had no effect on body rotation but increased ipsilateral step length. This study found bilateral DNa02 inhibition decreases step length bilaterally, as does bilateral DNa01 inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claim C148 cites Yang et al., 2023. Claims C149-C150 are from this study's Figure 8H. The comparison highlights differences between unilateral and bilateral perturbations and between treadmill and freely walking conditions, as discussed by the authors.

results.result: Bilateral optogenetic inhibition of DNa01 decreased forward velocity, but electrophysiological results show DNa01 and DNa02 are only weakly correlated with forward velocity during normal locomotion. This suggests these DNs are normally recruited for steering control, but bilateral perturbations can produce forward velocity changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C153 reconcile apparently contradictory findings. C151 is from Figure 8H, C152 from earlier electrophysiology (Figure 2C), and C153 is a reasonable synthesis. The explanation that bilateral perturbations can have effects not seen during normal function is plausible.

results.result: Many DNs influence steering during walking. Optogenetic inhibition of DNa01 produced only small steering defects, and DNa02 inhibition had no significant effects, consistent with DNa02 being one of many steering DNs. Subsequent studies identified additional steering DNs including DNg13, DNb05, DNb06, DNa11, DNae003, DNa03, DNae014, and DNb02.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C159 are supported by this study's optogenetic results (Figure 8E) and citations to subsequent work (Yang et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2024; Braun et al., 2024). The modest effects of single DN perturbations are consistent with a distributed steering control system.

results.result: Some steering DNs are organized hierarchically, with 'broadcaster' DNs recruiting other DNs with specialized functions. DNa02 is downstream from DNa03 (promotes decreased forward speed and ipsiversive steering) and DNp09 (promotes increased forward speed and ipsiversive steering).
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C162 are supported by citations to Braun et al., 2024; Sapkal et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2024; Westeinde et al., 2024; Bidaye et al., 2020. This places the current findings in the context of emerging understanding of hierarchical organization in the descending control system.

results.result: DNs targeting wings and legs are largely distinct populations, and DNs for flight steering differ from those identified here. However, DNa02 has indirect connectivity to wing motor neurons suggesting flight steering contribution, and DNa03 activation promotes turning in both flight and walking. VES041 suppresses flight steering and is predicted to have a similar role during walking based on connectivity upstream from DNa02.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C167 are supported by citations (Namiki et al., 2018; Ros et al., 2024; Schnell et al., 2017; Cheong et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2024). Claim C168 is an inference from connectome data that is reasonable but untested. The discussion appropriately distinguishes between established findings and predictions.

results.result: Clear responses to lateralized sensory stimuli were observed in steering DNs even when the fly was not walking. Similarly, Drosophila landing DNs respond to visual stimuli when not flying. These residual DN responses can be thought of as latent bias toward action or preparation for action that doesn't occur.
results.evaluation: Claim C169 is from this study's Figure 6. Claim C170 cites Ache et al., 2019. Claim C171 is an interpretation supported by citation to Kien, 1990. The concept of latent motor commands is interesting and well-supported, though alternative explanations (small undetected movements) cannot be fully excluded.

results.result: Mammalian corticospinal neurons can be active without movement, during movement preparation or observation. These latent signals may represent movement preparation and drive latent spinal neuron activity. The discovery of latent motor activity in Drosophila provides a starting point for mechanistic investigations of motor preparation.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C173 cite relevant mammalian literature (Tanji and Evarts, 1976; Kraskov et al., 2014; Churchland et al., 2010; Prut and Fetz, 1999). Claim C174 is a reasonable forward-looking statement about the potential of the Drosophila system for studying motor preparation, given the genetic and connectomic tools available.

results.result: Behavioral state transitions may be organized via pre-DN networks in the lateral accessory lobe. DNa03 and LAL010 receive bilateral input from PFL2 and VES041, cell types known for high-level premotor control. LAL013, another pre-DN with similar connectivity, plays an important role in modulating steering.
results.evaluation: Claim C175 cites Namiki and Kanzaki, 2016. Claims C176-C177 are supported by connectome analysis and citations (Westeinde et al., 2024; Ros et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2024). This highlights the importance of pre-DN networks in steering control.

results.result: Steering is driven by combinations of DNs with distinct functional roles, recruited by distinct parallel pathways in the brain, and targeting largely non-overlapping sets of cells in the ventral cord.
results.evaluation: Claim C178 is a high-level summary of the paper's main findings, well-supported by the combined electrophysiological and connectomic evidence presented throughout.

results.result: Any walking organism faces the same basic physical constraints, so evolution likely found common solutions. Recent work has begun identifying vertebrate steering DNs. Based on these results, vertebrate steering DNs should also be diverse and specialized.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C180 cite Dickinson et al., 2000 for the principle of common physical constraints. Claim C181 cites vertebrate work (Cregg et al., 2020; Usseglio et al., 2020). Claim C182 is a reasonable prediction based on the Drosophila findings, though it remains to be tested.

results.result: Orienting behaviors are fundamental indicators of an organism's perceptions and intentions, providing a window into perception and cognition. Understanding DN specializations should allow reframing orientation control as a problem of generating specific DN dynamics, enabling understanding of sensory and cognitive computations as solutions to dynamical system control problems.
results.evaluation: Claims C183-C184 state general principles about the importance of orienting behaviors. Claims C185-C186 are forward-looking statements about how understanding motor control neurons can inform understanding of upstream sensory and cognitive processes. These are reasonable perspectives supported by the study's findings, though they represent a conceptual framework rather than tested hypotheses.

results.result: DNa01 and DNa02 project to leg neuromeres in the ventral nerve cord, forming selective connections onto leg-control networks. DNa02 makes more direct synaptic connections onto motor neurons compared to DNa01, and very few postsynaptic cells are shared between the two DN types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these anatomical findings without challenge. The editor notes the work characterizes 'two types of descending neurons (DNs) that connect the brain to motor units,' and Reviewer 3 highlights the connectome data showing 'largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord.' These anatomical claims are accepted as foundational to the study.

results.result: Both DNa01 and DNa02 are depolarized before ipsilateral steering and hyperpolarized when the fly stops moving. DNa02 exhibits more transient fluctuations and is recruited earlier than DNa01, with spike rate fluctuations in DNa02 typically preceding those in DNa01.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 praises the 'technically impressive' in-vivo recordings and notes that 'DNa02 predicts transient turns DNa01 predicts slow sustained turns.' Reviewer 1 describes the experiments as 'well-designed and controlled.' The temporal dynamics and differential recruitment patterns are accepted as compelling evidence for distinct functional roles.

results.result: DNa01 and DNa02 firing rate increases are followed by changes in rotational and sideways velocity but not consistently in forward velocity. Steering filters are larger for DNa02 than DNa01, suggesting DNa02 operates with higher gain. DNa02 filters are biphasic while DNa01 filters are monophasic, indicating DNa02 produces more transient steering changes and provides better behavioral predictions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 emphasizes that the recordings 'provide a much higher resolution DN characterization' and notes the distinct functional profiles are well-supported. The editor highlights that the work shows DNs are 'involved in different aspects of turning control.' These filter analyses and gain differences are accepted as key evidence for functional specialization.

results.result: Rotational velocity is consistently related to the difference in right-left DNa02 firing rates in a linear relationship across the dynamic range, consistent during both forward and backward walking. Similar results were obtained for DNa01. Predictions from simultaneously recorded right-left pairs accurately predict turns in both directions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically highlights the 'simultaneous recordings from bilateral DNs (Fig. 3)' as 'especially impressive,' noting they 'show clearly that DNa02 cells not only fire more during ipsilateral turning events but that they get inhibited during contralateral turns.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes the importance of the statement that 'DNa02 activity was higher on the side ipsilateral to the attractive stimulus, but contralateral to the aversive stimulus' as 'really important - and only possible to see because of the dual recordings.'

results.result: Micro-stimulating PEN1 neurons causes EPG bump jumps, followed by compensatory behavioral turns in the correct direction to return the bump via the shortest path. DNa02 fires bursts before compensatory turns, predicts trial-to-trial variability in turn magnitude, and is recruited specifically on the side predicting turn direction. This demonstrates DNa02 activity predicts steering maneuvers guided by the head direction system.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 describes the 'experiment in Figure 4' as 'elegant' and notes the authors 'put a lot of effort into ensuring that ATP puffs do not accidentally activate the DNs.' Reviewer 3 calls this 'another technical feat' that 'provided a way to causally relate changes in the head-direction system to DNa02 activity.' The editor notes the work shows 'orientation signals act by preferentially increasing relative stimulation onto left- or right-turn-inducing DNs.'

results.result: Lateralized fictive odor stimuli produce asymmetric DNa02 responses with higher firing on the ipsilateral side and contralateral hyperpolarization, while fictive heat stimuli produce higher firing contralateral to the stimulus. DNa02 activity is higher ipsilateral to attractive stimuli but contralateral to aversive stimuli, encoding the laterality of the stimulus-evoked action rather than the stimulus itself. DNa02 is activated ~150ms before stimulus-evoked turns and predicts trial-to-trial variability.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically highlights the finding that 'DNa02 activity was higher on the side ipsilateral to the attractive stimulus, but contralateral to the aversive stimulus' as 'really important.' Reviewer 2 also notes the 'idea that different sensory cues can converge on a common motor program' where 'the turn-toward or turn-away mechanism is initiated by valence rather than whether the stimulus was odor or temperature' is 'of particular interest.'

results.result: DNa02 hyperpolarizes when the fly stops walking but continues responding to lateralized odors during immobility with similar stimulus-evoked firing rate changes as during walking. This suggests DNa02 contains information about latent steering drives even in quiescent behavioral states.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations about latent activity. The findings are consistent with the broader acceptance of DNa02's role in encoding steering commands, and no concerns are raised about the interpretation of activity during immobility.

results.result: The inputs to DNa02 are largely non-overlapping with those of DNa01, and they have largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord. Both receive substantial input from central brain intrinsic neurons, but only DNa02 receives direct input from PFL3 cells. This suggests they represent parallel and largely independent pathways for steering control.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes that 'connectome data shows these two DNs receive largely non-overlapping inputs in the brain, and they have largely non-overlapping outputs in the ventral nerve cord.' The editor acknowledges the work characterizes DNs 'involved in different aspects of turning control.' These connectome findings are accepted as supporting the functional specialization observed in electrophysiology.

results.result: PFL3 cells compare head direction with internal goal signals and produce directional steering commands when mismatched. PFL3 neurons are the likely origin of turning signals in DNa02 during head direction system perturbations. PFL3 sends both direct and strong indirect projections to DNa02 via DNa03 and LAL010, and also projects to cells that inhibit contralateral copies of DNa02, DNa03, and LAL010. This architecture suggests a 'see-saw' model of steering with opposite effects on the two copies of DNa02.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes that 'the insights on the pre-synaptic side - how sensory and central complex heading circuits converge onto these DNs is stronger' than motor-side insights. Reviewer 2 also comments that 'the "see-saw", where left-right symmetry is broken to allow a turn, presumably by excitation on one side and inhibition of the other leg motor modules, is interesting but not well explained here.' While the see-saw mechanism needs better explanation, the connectivity patterns themselves are accepted.

results.result: Some indirect connections onto DNa02 are bilaterally symmetric. DNa03 and LAL010 receive strong bilaterally symmetric projections from PFL2, which is recruited when the fly is oriented away from its internal goal and increases overall steering gain without specifying turn direction.
results.evaluation: These connectome findings are presented alongside the see-saw model and are not challenged by reviewers. They are accepted as part of the broader connectivity analysis showing how different pathways contribute to steering control.

results.result: Multiple pathways connect olfactory and thermosensory peripheral cells to DNa02, with the shortest involving MBON32. MBON32 projections are organized for see-saw steering and could drive turning toward appetitive stimuli or away from aversive stimuli. This is explained by parallel plastic excitatory and fixed inhibitory pathways to MBON32, where depression of KC→MBON32 synapses by aversive stimuli unmasks inhibition.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes the 'idea that different sensory cues can converge on a common motor program' is 'of particular interest.' The connectome-based model for valence-dependent steering through MBON32 plasticity is accepted as consistent with the experimental observations of opposite DNa02 responses to attractive versus aversive stimuli.

results.result: DNa02 receives abundant visual input from multiple sources: visual projection neurons from the optic lobe, projection neurons in the anterior optic tubercle downstream from LC10 cells (small object motion detectors), and via MBON32 which receives visual input in addition to olfactory and thermosensory input.
results.evaluation: These connectome findings are not challenged by reviewers and are accepted as part of the comprehensive characterization of DNa02 inputs showing integration of multiple sensory modalities.

results.result: DNa02 is a site of integration for many steering control pathways, which tend to be arranged for see-saw steering control (when one copy is excited, the other is inhibited). Many pathways involve parallel excitation and inhibition, which could provide a mechanism to specify steering direction based on E/I balance.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes the see-saw model is 'interesting but not well explained here' and that 'how hyperpolarization affects motor outputs is not clear.' However, the basic connectivity patterns supporting the see-saw architecture are accepted. The mechanistic details need clarification, but the anatomical organization is not disputed.

results.result: Unilateral optogenetic activation of DNa02 evoked a small but statistically significant steering bias in the ipsilateral direction, larger than expected by chance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these optogenetic activation results. Reviewer 2 notes the 'gain-of-function experiments in freely walking flies' are part of the technically impressive dataset. The modest effect size is consistent with the interpretation that DNa02 is one of many steering DNs.

results.result: Inhibiting DNa01 significantly reduced sideways speed and produced defects in inner-back-leg stance prolongation, while rotational speed was unchanged when either DNa01 or DNa02 were inhibited. A similar trend for stance prolongation defects was observed with DNa02 inhibition but fell short of statistical significance. This suggests defects in specific leg maneuvers are compensated via other mechanisms to achieve normal body rotation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes that 'loss-of-function was tested but has minimal effect, which is not surprising in a system with partially redundant control mechanisms.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges that 'optogenetic activation or inactivation showed relatively subtle phenotypes for both neurons (consistent with data in other recent preprints, Yang et al 2023 and Feng et al 2024).' The modest loss-of-function effects are accepted as consistent with redundancy in the steering system.

results.result: Inhibiting either DNa01 or DNa02 altered leg movement rhythm (increased step length, decreased step frequency) regardless of walking direction. Inhibiting DNa01 also decreased forward velocity.
results.evaluation: These effects on leg kinematics are not challenged by reviewers and are accepted as part of the loss-of-function phenotype characterization. They contribute to understanding how these DNs influence motor output.

results.result: DNa01 and DNa02 are both recruited during turning bouts in walking flies, but have distinct functional profiles: DNa02 predicts large, rapid, transient steering events and is recruited earlier, while DNa01 predicts smaller, slower steering events. These results argue that the two DNs play specialized roles in steering control.
results.evaluation: The editor states the work shows DNs are 'involved in different aspects of turning control.' Reviewer 3 notes the 'electrophysiological results in this study support this hypothesis: these two DN types have distinct functional profiles.' The functional specialization is accepted as a major finding, though Reviewer 3 notes 'the role of DNa01 on the other hand seems unclear based on physiology, optogenetics perturbations as well as connectome analysis.'

results.result: Optogenetically inhibiting DNa01 produced only small defects in steering, and inhibiting DNa02 did not produce statistically significant effects on steering.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states this is 'not surprising in a system with partially redundant control mechanisms.' Reviewer 3 notes these results are 'consistent with data in other recent preprints, Yang et al 2023 and Feng et al 2024.' The modest loss-of-function effects are accepted as expected given the redundancy in the steering system.

results.result: Subsequent studies (Yang et al. 2023, Feng et al. 2024, Braun et al. 2024) confirmed key findings: unilateral DNa02 excitation produces ipsilateral rotation, bilateral DNa02 ablation reduces corrective turning velocity, bilateral activation can drive turning in either direction, and DNa02 perturbation mainly affects ipsilateral leg movements. The brain connectome analyses explain how DNa02 activity correlates with both ipsi- and contralateral legs through see-saw arrangement. DNa01 and DNa02 are normally recruited for steering control, though bilateral perturbations can produce forward velocity changes.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly notes 'these compelling results, together with the independent work that they have inspired, represent significant progress.' Reviewer 2 states the 'data is also consistent with/complementary to subsequent manuscripts (Yang 2023, Feng 2024, and Ros 2024).' The convergence of findings across multiple independent studies strongly supports the main conclusions.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on anatomical claims C1, C2, C6, C7. Both evaluations accept the connectome-based characterization of distinct projection patterns and synaptic targets for the two DN types as foundational and well-supported.

Strong agreement on electrophysiological findings (C8-C11). OpenEval emphasizes temporal dynamics and correlation patterns; peer reviewers praise the 'technically impressive' recordings and accept the differential recruitment patterns as compelling evidence for distinct functional roles. Peer review also includes C20-C21 on temporal precedence.

Agreement on linear filter analysis (C12-C19) and gain analysis (C24-C26). OpenEval finds the computational analysis methodologically sound; peer reviewers emphasize the 'higher resolution DN characterization' and accept the distinct functional profiles as well-supported.

Partial overlap on temporal precedence claims C20-C21. OpenEval groups these with synthesis claims C22-C23; peer review includes them with electrophysiology results. Both accept the temporal dynamics as well-documented.

Partial overlap on gain analysis (C24-C26). OpenEval notes the analysis would benefit from quantitative slope comparisons; peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the broader functional specialization evidence without raising concerns.

Strong agreement on bilateral recording findings (C27-C32). OpenEval notes the linear relationship is well-characterized; peer reviewers specifically highlight these 'especially impressive' dual recordings showing ipsilateral excitation and contralateral inhibition as key technical achievements.

OpenEval evaluates claims C35-C38 about EPG neurons and central complex connectivity as supported by citations and prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background/hypothesis claims.

Partial overlap on head direction system claims. OpenEval evaluates C39-C44 including background knowledge and negative controls; peer review focuses on the experimental validation (C43-C60) and praises the 'technical feat' of causally relating head-direction changes to DNa02 activity.

Partial overlap on compensatory turn experiments (C45-C50). OpenEval finds directional specificity well-documented; peer reviewers emphasize the elegant experimental design and causal relationship established through careful controls.

Partial overlap on DNa02 activation during head direction experiments (C51-C57). OpenEval emphasizes temporal sequence and predictive power; peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the broader head direction experiment validation.

Partial overlap on synthesis of head direction findings (C58-C60). OpenEval notes direct causal manipulation would strengthen conclusions; peer reviewers accept the functional strength of the pathway as demonstrated.

Partial overlap on olfactory/thermal stimulus responses (C61-C65). OpenEval finds behavioral and neural responses consistent with prior work; peer reviewers do not challenge these observations and accept them as part of the sensory integration characterization.

Partial overlap on valence-dependent responses (C66-C69). OpenEval emphasizes this as key evidence that DNa02 encodes action direction rather than stimulus location; peer reviewers specifically highlight this finding as 'really important' for understanding motor program convergence.

Partial overlap on temporal precedence and predictive power for sensory responses (C70-C73). OpenEval notes similarity between DNa01 and DNa02 responses; peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the broader sensory integration evidence.

Perfect agreement on latent activity during immobility (C74-C77). OpenEval finds the interpretation as latent steering drives reasonable while acknowledging alternative explanations; peer reviewers do not challenge these observations.
OpenEval evaluates synthesis claims C78-C81 about multimodal input convergence as well-supported by multiple experiments. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific synthesis.

Strong agreement on non-overlapping inputs (C82-C85). OpenEval notes these explain functional differences; peer reviewers accept the connectome data showing 'largely non-overlapping inputs' as supporting the functional specialization observed in electrophysiology.

Partial overlap on PFL3 connectivity (C86-C88). OpenEval finds the inference about PFL3 as origin of turning signals reasonable; peer reviewers note the pre-synaptic insights are strong and accept the connectivity patterns, though note the see-saw mechanism needs better explanation.

Strong agreement on see-saw model (C89-C96). OpenEval finds the model well-supported by connectivity and experimental observations; peer reviewers accept the connectivity patterns but note the mechanism is 'interesting but not well explained' and that 'how hyperpolarization affects motor outputs is not clear.'

Perfect agreement on PFL2 bilateral connectivity (C97-C100). OpenEval notes this contrasts with asymmetric PFL3 connections; peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the comprehensive connectivity analysis without challenge.

Partial overlap on MBON32 connectivity (C101-C104). OpenEval finds the see-saw organization consistent with PFL3 pattern; peer reviewers accept the connectivity supporting valence-dependent steering through MBON32 plasticity.
